summary: This RFC describes the Exterior Gateway Protocol used to connect stub gateways to an autonomous system of core gateways. It specifies the working protocol and defines it as an official ARPA protocol. It is an early stage in how Internet routing between systems developed.

eli5.summary: Small neighborhood roads need a way to tell the main highway which addresses they can reach. This protocol is how those little roads report in.

questions: what is the stub exterior gateway protocol
how did stub gateways connect to the core
how do egp neighbors check reachability
what is an egp network reachability message
subtitle: How a stub gateway tells the core of the Internet which networks it can reach, and checks that its neighbor is still alive.

tldr.problem: As the DARPA Catenet grew, running one routing algorithm across every gateway became too costly, too hard to maintain and too rigid. Separate autonomous systems needed a way to exchange reachability information without sharing an algorithm.
tldr.mechanism: EGP has three parts: a two-way handshake to become neighbors, Hello and I Heard You messages to check that a neighbor is reachable, and polled Network Reachability messages that list the networks a gateway is a good first hop for.
tldr.outcome: RFC 888 defined an official ARPA protocol for stub gateways to attach to the core system. It is not itself a routing algorithm, and it was later updated by RFC 904.

today: The metadata lists this RFC as updated by RFC 904. The text itself describes the protocol as the working, official ARPA protocol of January 1984 and does not say what happened to it afterward.

sections.title: Why Split the Internet into Autonomous Systems
sections.content:
The DARPA Catenet was expected to keep growing. RFC 888 lists three reasons why one routing algorithm shared by every gateway would become less and less feasible: the routing overhead grows too large, many very different gateways in a single algorithm make maintenance and fault isolation nearly impossible, and the software becomes too rigid because any change must be made in too many places by too many people.

The expected answer is a set of autonomous systems, each made of relatively homogeneous gateways. What a system runs inside itself is a private matter. In the simplest case a system is one stub gateway joining a local network to the ARPANET. The DARPA gateways on ARPANET and SATNET form the core system, used as a long-haul transport by the stub systems. The more general case of co-equal systems was still research, and this document covers only how stubs connect to the core.
sections.eli5: Instead of one giant rulebook for every road, each neighborhood keeps its own rules. The neighborhoods only need a simple way to talk to each other.

sections.title: Stubs, Neighbors and Autonomous Systems
sections.content:
A stub gateway is not a core gateway, shares a network with at least one core gateway, has interfaces to networks with no core gateways, and is the only path from the core to those other networks. A stub must fully run ICMP, including answering echo requests and sending destination dead and Redirect messages, as well as EGP.

Every EGP message header carries a 16-bit autonomous system number. Zero is never assigned and is reserved for future use. Two gateways with an interface on the same network are neighbors. If they belong to the same autonomous system they are interior neighbors; otherwise they are exterior neighbors.

EGP is a polling protocol, so each side controls how fast it sends and receives reachability information. All EGP messages travel a single hop, so the time-to-live should be very small, and each gateway keeps one sequence number per neighbor. EGP runs directly over IP as protocol number 8.
sections.eli5: Two houses on the same street are neighbors. If they belong to the same club they are club neighbors, and if not they are outside neighbors who only trade information when they ask for it.

sections.title: Neighbor Acquisition and Reachability
sections.content:
Gateways become direct neighbors with a standard two-way handshake. One sends a Neighbor Acquisition Request, repeated at a reasonable rate (perhaps every 30 seconds or so) until a Reply or a Refusal arrives. The receiver answers with a Reply, or optionally a Refusal with a reason. A Request and Reply also state the minimum interval the sender will accept between Hellos and between NR polls.

To stop being neighbors, a gateway sends a Neighbor Cease message, which the other side must acknowledge. A stub is configured with the addresses of no more than two or three core gateways to approach. If all its direct neighbors fail, it must acquire a new one.

To track liveness, a Hello must be answered promptly with an I Heard You, never more than a few seconds later. A core gateway declares a neighbor unreachable if, among its last n Hellos, it got fewer than k replies, and reachable again if it got at least j replies to its last m Hellos. The RFC deliberately does not fix n, m, k, j or the Hello frequency, because they depend on the neighbors and their network. An unreachable neighbor stays a direct neighbor, but after an extremely long time, such as an hour, the gateway should stop treating it as one.
sections.eli5: First you shake hands to agree to be neighbors. Then every so often one of you calls out hello and the other says I heard you, so you both know the other is still home.

sections.title: Network Reachability Messages and Polling
sections.content:
A gateway G is an appropriate first hop to network M, relative to network N, when traffic for M arriving over G's network N interface is forwarded without passing through another gateway on N. The NR message lists the networks for which the sender is an appropriate first hop, each with a distance. Core gateways report distances below 128 for networks reachable without leaving the core and 128 or above otherwise; a stub reports less than 128 for all of its networks. A distance of 255 means unreachable. If several successive NR messages omit a network, it is treated as no longer reachable.

Core gateways can also list their other neighbors on the network and the networks each is a first hop for. A stub sends the simplest message, a single block listing itself and the networks reachable only through it. A stub must never forward traffic to a core gateway that is not an appropriate first hop, except for datagrams using the source route option.

NR messages normally go out only in reply to an NR Poll. No gateway may poll more than once per minute, and polls may only be sent to neighbors declared reachable. A poll carries a sequence number that the reply repeats, and there is no provision for multiple outstanding polls to one neighbor. If no NR message arrives after the maximum retransmissions, the poller must assume the neighbor is not an appropriate first hop for any network. Between two polls, a gateway may send one unsolicited NR message with the unsolicited bit set.
sections.eli5: A gateway answers the question which addresses are best reached through you, along with how far each one is. You are only allowed to ask about once a minute, so nobody gets pestered.

sections.title: Indirect Neighbors and Limitations
sections.content:
Becoming a direct neighbor takes three steps: acquisition, reachability checks and periodic NR polling. If a neighbor G' reports other gateways that are better first hops for some networks, a gateway may send traffic straight to them. It is then an indirect neighbor of those gateways via G': it forwards to them but does no acquisition, Hello exchange or polling with them. If a later NR message from G' no longer mentions one of them, it is treated as unreachable.

EGP is not itself a routing algorithm. If the topology breaks the stub rules, it does not give enough information to prevent loops, and a gateway that falsely claims to be a first hop for a network can cause traffic for that network to never be delivered.
sections.eli5: If your neighbor tells you about a friend who has a shortcut, you can send mail straight to the friend without making friends with them first. But you have to trust what your neighbor tells you.

sections.title: EGP Message Formats
sections.content:
Appendix A defines five message families, all using EGP version 2 and carrying a one's complement checksum over the message and a 16-bit autonomous system number. The types are NR message (type 1), NR Poll (type 2), Neighbor Acquisition and Cease (type 3), Neighbor Hello and I Heard You (type 5), and an error message.

Within the acquisition type, the code selects Request (0), Reply (1), Refusal (2), Cease (3) or Cease Acknowledgment (4). Refusal reasons are unspecified, out of table space or administrative prohibition. Cease reasons are unspecified, going down or no longer needed. The Hello and I Heard You status field says whether the sender thinks the other side is reachable and, if not, why.
sections.eli5: Every EGP message starts with the same kind of label saying what sort of message it is, who sent it, and a check number to catch mistakes.
